title: The Ash Watch Night-Log
author: the keepers of Ash Watch, nine days each
body:
# Ash Watch: the night-log

*Kept in the Rest's four columns: the hour, the ground, what was seen, who saw it. Nothing is written that was not seen.*

---

**Third watch, Tallowday.** The bed. Nothing. Grey to the ninth waystone and green behind it, as it was. — *Brannock*

**Fourth watch, Tallowday.** The bed. A walker coming up the glass from the Choir side, an hour before light, slow. Grey from head to foot but upright, and walking the way a woman walks with a full jug, careful of the edges. — *Brannock*

**Fourth watch, Merrowday.** The same walker, the same hour. She went to the Wellspring and knelt at the lip and filled something and went back down. Behind her on the bed the grey came up after her, a stride at a time, the way a tide comes after a boat. I did not light the fire. A beacon is for a thing that is coming. She is going. — *Brannock*

**Fourth watch, Hushday.** She did not fill it. She left it on the lip, full, and stood. I lit the beacon. I do not know why. The book says to write that, so I have. — *Brannock*

**Morning, Hushday.** Relieved. The keeper Brannock says he did not light the fire. The fire is lit. — *Esk, for the Rest*

title: The Pinfold's Pound-Book
author: the hayward of Merrowby
body:
# The Pinfold, this spring

*One penny to ring the bell and take home what is yours.*

---

**Kindleday.** Two ewes, Tamwick mark, a hole and a slit. Paid. — **Tallowday.** A goat, nobody's, eats hats. Paid by the hatter.

**Merrowday.** One wether too many. Nobody put him in. Earmark: a notch under and a notch over, which is no mark I know. Unpaid.

**Thornday.** He is still here. And one more again this morning, the same mark. I have let the first one out on the Eastway. Unpaid.

**Skerrday.** The one I let out is back, or it is another. The mark is the same. I asked at Merrowby market and old Pellam said a notch under and a notch over was the Bramcombe mark before the Toll fell, the one on the wash-house beam up there, and nobody has cut it in two hundred years.

**Every day since.** One. Same mark. Unpaid. I have stopped letting him out. The bell has not been rung.

title: Keepers of Hound Watch
author: painted by the Rest's sign-writer, a line a keeper
body:
# Keepers of Hound Watch

*Nine years to a keeper. The bell is rung for the Choir, never at it.*

---

Orrin Ashby

Hesk Marrow the elder

*(scraped to the wood)*

Godwin Hale

Annet Rook

Ewan Pell

... and on down the board to the present keeper, who has chalked beside his own name, *they moved*.

---

*Pencilled on the back of the board, very small, in an old Warden's hand:* Dunnet Hale kept the watch nine years and a winter and rang the bell at the colossi one night and went down to see why. The Rest has taken his name off the board so that the next keeper does not think it is a thing a keeper does. We will say it once a year in the Roll room and not otherwise. He owed nobody anything. — H.

title: The Roll in Orm's Cist
author: the hand that burnt it, before the Wardens
body:
# The Roll in Orm's Cist

*Burnt into hide with a hot point, one line a hearth, older than the Wardens' Roll and older than the Toll. The Vale's names are nearly the Vale's names; the spelling has drifted, the places have not.*

---

**Merowbi**: forty hearths and the smith.

**Tamwic by the press**: nineteen hearths.

**Tamwic at the yew**: one hearth, and a bell in the sapling so it will be found.

**Cresburn**: the beds, eleven hearths.

**Harwel**: a hare cut on the well.

**Gosforde**: nine hearths at the ford.

---

*At the foot, in the same hot hand:* A hearth that is one is still a hearth. Say it with the others or it will not stay.

title: Levels at the Sedge Hearth
author: a junior Sayer of the Circle, unsigned
body:
# Levels at the Sedge Hearth

*Taken at dawn against the Hearth's own stone, which has not moved in three hundred years, and the water, which has. Figures in fingers.*

---

First week: the water stands eleven fingers under the stone's mark. The reeds west of the line are browning.

Second week: eleven and a half. The line has moved a pole's length toward the Eelweir.

Third week: twelve. I have taken up the plank so the Sedgehithe cutters will stop coming out to ask me what I am doing, because I do not know how to tell them.

Fourth week: twelve and a half. The line is not in the reeds. It is under them. Where the water has gone down there is a kerb of Builders' stone a hand under the silt, straight as a rule, running from the Sedgehithe bollards to the Eelweir, and reed will not root on it.

*Underneath, in the same hand, crossed out:* the Mere is draining along something. *And then, not crossed out:* The Circle says a measurement error. I have measured it twelve times.

title: The Dedication of the Long Stride
author: cut by the Builders; rubbed off the stone; construed, doubtfully, by Cassa Binder
body:
# The Dedication of the Long Stride

*Three lines on the hidden face of the last block in the Old Quarry, which was never lifted out and never laid. The face was cut before the block was.*

---

*First line.* A road across the water to the stone we set first.

*Second line.* Walk it by the lamps, which are names; each lamp is one who walked it for the first time.

*Third line.* The last stone is not laid. Walk it anyway. *(Or: The last stone is not laid, so that it may be walked. Or: so that it is always being walked. The verb is the one the Sayers call the held tense, and nobody agrees what it holds.)*

---

*Cassa's note.* The causeway has two hundred and six lamp-posts. The Guild says two hundred and five. They have never counted the one at the city end because it has never lit.

title: The Counting Tower Ledger, the last forty pages
author: not the clerk
body:
# The Counting Tower Ledger

*Carts down out of Skerrow, counted at the window, for the Guild.*

---

The clerk's entries stop in the middle of a Hushday: *three carts ore, one cart bone, one herd* — and a blot.

After the blot the ledger goes on in figures the clerk does not use: the Builders' numerals, a stroke and a ring and a stroke, the ones cut on the Narrows Bridge and the Stair Bridge and the Long Stride, which the Sayers read and nobody else does.

They are counting carts, as the clerk did, at the same window, at the same hours. But the tally is kept against a column the Guild's ledgers do not have, headed with one Oroth word the Circle renders as *owed back*.

*Pencilled at the foot of the last page, in the clerk's own hand, shaking:* I have not counted since the pins began to come out. It counts. I sit at the window and it counts.

title: A Chart of the Western Water
author: a Salt Isles pilot, unsigned
body:
# A Chart of the Western Water

*Greased sailcloth; the coasts drawn as rows of bells, the depths as bell-counts. The legend is in the Salt Isles' script, which the reedfolk of Oulea can still half read.*

---

The Isles, at the left edge: seven of them, each a bell.

The water between: bell-counts, falling as it comes east, which means the water is shallowing.

The coast of Wickmere, at the right edge: not drawn as bells, as every other coast is, but as a line of small footprints.

And a road across the water from the Isles to the footprints, straight, cut in the pilot's hand with a knife rather than drawn, and at the Wickmere end, where the Builders' Harbour stands on the Ash Strand, one word the Oulea women read as *due*.

title: Beyond the Northern Gate
author: the chart-maker of the Circle's Listeners, 1038
body:
# Beyond the Northern Gate

*Soundings and bearings, kept for the Circle. The report will say what the Circle wishes to hear. This is what I measured.*

---

**First day.** Through the gate at dawn, the Wold's woman left at the stone behind us. The road goes on as a road. The thorn is thick on the far side too; it is not a wall, it is a hedge, and we are in the field.

**Second day.** The road goes down. By noon we could smell the sea, which is not possible; there is no sea north of the Wold on any chart in the Spire.

**Third day.** It is not a sea. It is a shore with no water, a strand of grey sand going down, and the tide-lines on it are fresh every morning, and there is nothing to have left them. We took soundings of nothing. I have written them down.

**Fourth day.** We came back. The road was cleared ahead of us all the way to the gate, the stones carried off it, though nobody passed us. The Listeners have agreed what we will report. I have agreed to say nothing, and I am putting this in the trunk, because the Wold's woman does not open things, and she will keep it.

title: Kharrow's Cairns: the Names
author: the memory-keepers of Clan Kharrow
body:
# The names at Kharrow's Cairns

*Every Kharrow the mountain has kept, one line each, sung once a year at the cairns by whoever keeps the memory.*

---

... and on down the slate, eleven hundred lines, the oldest recut, the spellings drifting as the singers drift.

**Harl ko-Kharrow**, who went up the Cradle after the lost herd in the winter of the long snow and was not brought down.

---

*Scratched beside that line, small, in Ushka ko-Kharrow's hand, forty years ago:* not in the song. I have sung every line on this slate for forty-one years and I have never sung this one, and I do not know why my mouth will not. Somebody go up the Cradle and ask him.

title: The Day-Book of the Greyfold Run
author: Tam Oakes, carter, of Larkbourne Ford
body:
# The Greyfold run

*Carter's day-book. Loads out, loads in, what was paid.*

---

**Tallowday.** Six sacks barley, two of salt, to the waystation. Grey on the road from the ninth stone. Paid.

**Thornday.** Same load. The ash is falling like a snow that does not melt. Paid, but the waystation keeper's hands shook.

**Hushday.** Greyfold's order: bread, salt, a knife for the Fallows' boy, a shoe for the little one who lost hers in the lane. The road is gone under the ash past the waystation. I walked it in. The tables were laid and there was nobody. I put the order on the tables. Not paid.

**The next Hushday.** Greyfold's order, the same. I do not know who ordered it. I walked it in. Nobody. The order from last week was gone off the tables.

**Every Hushday since.** The same. I have stopped writing the date. I have stopped going home. The carts are in the yard. I walk the order in on my back. *(The hand stops mid-line.)*

title: Manifest of the Kindly, Tollmere to the Ash Strand
author: the Guild's clerk at the timber quay
body:
# Manifest: the barge Kindly

*Out of Tollmere, timber quay, by the western water round the Tideflats to the Ash Strand, the Stride's toll on this load being dearer than the sea's.*

---

**For:** Wat Thatcher, sutler, Pilgrim's Ash, on account of the Tolling Order.

**Cargo, sealed:** grey cloth, forty bolts. Candles, tallow, twelve gross. Ash-cake flour, thirty sacks. Cooking pots, iron, twenty. Bells, small, hand, two hundred, *for the White Wood*.

**Crew:** four, lakefolk, named, paid half before sailing.

**Landing:** the strand beacon, by night, as agreed; the beacon to be lit by the sutler's man.

*Endorsed at the foot in the Guild clerk's hand:* sutler's man never known to the Guild. Paid in advance.

title: Three Stones, Three Readings
author: a Merrowby shepherd, on the back of a rubbing
body:
# Three stones, three readings

The Sayer who came in spring read the three pieces of the Toll's crown together and said it was one word, *hold*.

The Warden who came after read them the other way round and said it was a name, and would not say whose.

My ewes sleep against them every night because they are warm. I have rubbed all three, and laid the rubbings side by side in the lambing shed, and in the dark the charcoal shows a fourth piece between the second and the third that is on no stone. I have not told the Sayer. The ewes knew already.

title: Along the Hem of a Loaf-Cloth
author: the Chalk Cell's hermit, or somebody who used her window
body:
# Along the hem

*Written round the edge of the cloth, so the words go round and round the crust.*

Thirty years you brought bread and never asked my name and I never gave it, and it was the best bargain in the Vale. — I have watched the Spire across the water every day of forty years. This spring its crown turned a quarter toward the Vale and has not turned back. I would like my bread again, please, for a while. I am not finished watching. — *Leave it on the sill. Do not knock.*

title: Notice, Nailed to a Stake
author: the Guild's surveyor, for Tollmere
body:
# Notice

*To whom it concerns on Bram Down.*

The Guild has had the chalk of this pit weighed at the Limekilns and finds it the whitest in the Vale. The Guild proposes to take it by the cartload, at the Guild's price, for the white walls of Tollmere, which are presently being limed with chalk from the Whitecut that is coming up grey.

Objections to the Stride's Foot, in writing, within the month.

---

*Written under it in a Rookdown hand, pressed hard:* Rookdown cobs its houses with this chalk. It is not for sale. It is our walls. — *And under that, fainter:* and it is the only white thing left on the Brow.

title: Stars at Noon
author: a Barrow Down shepherd, on paper round a tally
body:
# Stars at noon

We have stopped mentioning it, which is how a shepherd says a thing is true.

On still days at noon the dew pond shows stars. Not the sky; the stars behind it. Always the same ones, low in the south, over the Hush, where there are no stars in the real sky at noon or at midnight.

The flock drinks from it anyway. The pond has never been seen empty or filling, and now it has been seen full of night. I have notched the days on the stick. Forty-one. The same number of cracks the miller's girl counts on the Toll. I do not like that I noticed.

title: On a Page Torn from a Tally-Book
author: unsigned; the hand is neither Vale nor Wold
body:
# On the torn page

Vale folk touch the hare going in and Woodfolk touch the leaf coming out, and nobody has ever been seen to touch both. — I have.

The bell on the top is for the ones who are neither: the pilgrims who walk south through the downs from the Wold, and there are more of them every year, and the stone had nothing for them to touch.

I have left the chisel. If anybody wants to cut a fourth mark, for whoever comes after the pilgrims, it is sharp enough.

title: Inside the Knot
author: a reedfolk hand, in Valish letters learned late
body:
# Inside the knot

*The name is not written. What is written is this.*

For the one who went down the Builders' steps from the Brow into the grey and did not come up, whose people are Vale and would not sing for him, because the Vale does not sing, it says names.

We do not know your name. We have lit you a light anyway, on the last step, because a light is how the reedfolk say it, and we did not think you would mind which way it was said.

— *Nauvissa, who cut the grey reed for the wick.*

title: One Line of the Deep Lines
author: a Warden of the Rest, copying
body:
# From the deep lines

*The name, the place, who spoke for them, the season it was read.*

**Wenna Tollhook**, Larkstead, spoken for by nobody, read at the first Candle Night the Rest kept.

---

*Under it, in the same hand:* A Merrowby child said this name out loud between the stones on Tollday, on a clear evening, the way the Vale says one name before it turns for home. She did not learn it from anybody. Larkstead was known for its singing, the Roll says, and stopped. The child sings. I have told her mother nothing and copied the line so that I would have it on me.

title: Received, for Mortar
author: Hallam Ashdown's apprentice, for the Pennywort family
body:
# Received

One hod lime mortar, the stone in the parapet to be set fast again, for Osric Pennywort, paid.

---

*Written on the back:* Set it fast on Merrowday. Tollday it had turned a quarter again, the same way, sunwise, like a stone grinding with nothing to grind. The mortar was on the road in a line of dust as fine as flour. Master says leave it. The mill's first stone cracked on its first turn and was built into the bridge so the Larkbourne would carry the bad luck to the Mere. Master says if it wants to turn, it has earned it.

title: Twenty Years Up the Ridge Road
author: Dorrie Cooper, carter, Tamwick-born, of Grandfather Hollow
body:
# Up the ridge road

*What went on the cart at the bottom, what the beam said at the bottom, what the Woodfolk scale said at the top.*

---

Twenty years of it. Rope, candles, cider up; moss, fungus, thorn down.

The beam says nothing is lost between the bottom and the top. The Woodfolk scale says nothing is lost. My slate says a cart and a half, in twenty years, a little every trip: not stolen, not spilt, just less at the top than at the bottom by a weight neither scale is fine enough to take.

The ridge road goes up past the Hare Stone. I have started saying my load aloud at the stone going up, item by item. The slate says it helps.

title: Knotted in Straw
author: a Brow shepherd, knotted, and read aloud by whoever finds it
body:
# Knotted in straw

*Shepherds on the Brow knot a count in straw when they have no knife. The knots say:*

One ewe. One night. The door kept shut on the Choir side. The ash swept off the step so the next one would know somebody had stayed.

*And a last knot, loose, the kind a shepherd ties when he is not sure:* The last one who grazed within sight of the Choir left this hut. I have come back to it. I do not know yet whether that means I am brave or that I have been called. The door stays facing away.

title: The Bell-Book, This Spring
author: the youngest at the Rest
body:
# Tollday bells

*Nine bells, rung in order, first to ninth, by the youngest.*

---

Kindleday: nine. Rung well.

Tollday: nine, and the ninth rang again after I had put it down. I thought it was the wind.

Tollday: nine, and the ninth rang again. There was no wind. I put my hand on it and it was ringing under my hand.

Tollday: I did not ring them. I have told Sergeant Dole it is my knee. — *Under it, in Dole's hand:* The first Wardens are buried together so they could keep the Roll room in sight. If one of them is ringing back, lad, he is answering you. Ring them.

title: The Barge's Last Load
author: the Woodfolk who loaded her, and later hands
body:
# The last load

*Notched in bark.* Eleven trunks of oak, each one asked, for the city, to be paid on landing.

---

*Cut into the kelson under the tally, in a Tallyman's letters:* Not delivered. Not paid for. 1005.

*Scratched beside that, with a knife, in a Woodfolk hand:* Not paid for. Not delivered.

*And at the foot, much older than either, burnt into the wood of the kelson itself where nobody could have reached to burn it after the barge was built:* an oak leaf. The oak that grows through her hold is older than the barge. The kelson was cut from its own acorn.

title: Ground at Brindle Mill
author: the clanless miller of Brindle Mill
body:
# Ground this week

Barley, Brindle, four sacks. Barley, Ghast, two. Oats, the tinkers, one, paid in a mended pot.

---

*Under the line:* The wheel turns against the water now. I have not changed the gearing. The beck runs uphill for a stride below the race and then remembers itself. The flour comes out the same. — I am clanless. I have no verse in the Rope-Song and no clan to ask. So I am asking the board: if the water is going back up the beck, where is it going? — *Somebody has chalked, small, in the corner:* home.

title: The Twelve Notes of the Toll, as Tuned
author: a tuner of the Sayers' Circle
body:
# The twelve buoys

*Each tuned to a note of the Toll's hum as the Circle took it in 1011, to prove the Bell account.*

First to twelfth, the chord.

---

*Pencilled under the chord:* Rowed out this spring to check them. Eleven are true to the card. The twelfth has gone flat by a quarter-tone, and it is the only one of the twelve that nobody has touched in thirty years, because it is moored nearest the Undercroft and the tuners do not like the water there.

The Toll's hum has gone down a quarter-tone this spring. The twelfth buoy knew first. That proves nothing to anyone's satisfaction, including mine.

title: Read at the End of the Dry Jetty
author: an eel-wife of Gullhithe
body:
# At the end of the jetty

*The eel-wives walk out along the old landing at dusk, where the Mere used to reach, and say the boats' names that went out from it.*

The Gull. The Two Sisters. The Wick. The Lettie, that was my mother's. The Tamsin.

---

*Written later, the hand shaking:* The last pile is wet to the knee every morning and the hayfield round it is dry. I put my hand on the wet and it was lake water, cold, with the smell of the deep. The Mere is two hundred yards off and falling. Something is still tying up here at night.

title: Toll, the Ness, First Night
author: a Guild clerk with no warrant
body:
# Toll, the Ness

*Every fish sold on the Ness to pay the city toll, by order of the Guild, from tonight.*

---

No sales entered. No boats landed at the tip. The fishers landed at the root instead, forty yards back, where the Ness is still the Vale's, and sold from there, and looked at me.

*At the foot, in the clerk's hand, smaller:* I was told there was a warrant. There is no warrant. I have been a clerk eleven years and I have never been looked at by a whole market before. I am going back to the Foot. Somebody may have the ledger. It is empty. It is the most honest page I have kept.

title: Knots of the Net Field
author: a net-mender of Gullhithe, in knots and a few words
body:
# The knot-book

*Mere knots, row by row: the sheet, the lake-bend, the Wick hitch.*

*Last row:* the Sedgish knot, three times, tied fast and small by fingers that knew it in the dark.

---

*Chalked on the canvas under it:* A net came back from the water mended with these, in the night, by nobody in Gullhithe. We cut the Sedgish ones out; we always do. This time I have kept them on the book. The mending was better than ours. — Whoever it was mends nets under the water. I would like to know what they catch.

title: Cut for the Smokehouses
author: the coppicers of the Smoke Coppice
body:
# Cut for the smokehouses

*Stools cut in their turn, oak for the pike.*

---

The old stool by the ditch, cut last winter, as it has been every ninth winter since before the Charter.

It has put up one shoot overnight, as thick as a man's arm, straight, with bark on it already, and leaves the size of a hand. We have not cut it. We will not cut it.

*Under that, the single word, underlined:* LISTENING. — *The coppicers will not say who wrote it. The shoot leans toward the Wold, the way the elder at Elderhold is said to lean.*

title: Readings at the Strandline
author: the Sayers' Circle, a hundred years of readers
body:
# The strandline

*Where the water stood the year the Toll fell, marked by three stones. The Mere's level against them, read each spring.*

---

For a hundred years the same figure, spring after spring, in forty different hands.

*This spring:* one finger lower. The first change in a century.

*Below, a reader's note:* The Sayers say the Mere is draining; the Lakefolk say it is resting. A finger is not an argument. I have put the rod back in the same hole and I will come back next spring, and so will whoever reads after me, and one of us will be the one who knows.

title: The Pitch of the Hum
author: the clerk at the Listening Post, for Ismay Ondrael
body:
# The pitch of the hum

*Taken every night at the horn, against the Circle's pipe.*

---

Forty-one years, and the figure moves by a hair a year, downward, which is the whole of Ismay Ondrael's account in one column.

*Then one night, underlined twice:* The hum changed pitch between the second and third readings. Not a hair. A step. I took it four more times. — That was the night, the Wardens say, that somebody came up the Hushline Stair.

*At the foot:* I cannot sing. I have never wished I could until tonight.

title: Worked in the Collar
author: a laundress of Tollmere, pencilled
body:
# In the collar

*Worked in blue thread, small, the way a mother marks a child's shirt:* Tessane.

---

*Pencilled inside the band:* None of us brought it. It came up on the third stone with the soft water, clean already. The Circle unsaid a Tessane, the old laundresses say, a hundred years back, and it worked. — I have cut the band off to keep and let the shirt go back in the water. I do not know why. A name in a collar is a thing you do not throw away, in the Vale or anywhere.

title: One Day Too Many
author: the crew of an eel-boat of Isseva, notched
body:
# One day too many

*The pole counts lifts. A boat lifts a hundred and forty traps a day.*

---

We went under the arch the wrong way at dusk because the channel was quicker and nobody has ever done it and nobody has ever said why not.

We came out at dawn. The pole has a whole day's lifts on it, a hundred and forty notches, cut by our knives, that none of us remembers cutting. Our beards say a day. The eels in the hold say a day.

We have gone back under it the right way, for luck, three times. The notches have not gone.

title: The Milestone at the Lowest Tide
author: a reedfolk girl of Oulea, wading
body:
# The milestone

*The Builders' road goes straight out of the carr into the sea. At the lowest tide a stone showed that nobody had seen, with a number.*

---

The number is a Builders' number, a stroke and a ring and a stroke, the ones on the Narrows Bridge. Meo Sa says it is a count down, like the Last Milestone in the ash, one, then none.

This one is not counting down. It is counting up. It says how far there is still to go, the Sayers would say, if a Sayer would wade.

*Underneath:* I waded. My feet were dry when I came out. The water was over my knees.

title: To the Reed Council, Unsent
author: the eel-trappers of the Eel Hurdles
body:
# To the Council

*The hurdles steer the eels into the traps as they run up from the sea. That is what hurdles are for.*

---

Every morning the traps are full and every eel in them is swimming the wrong way, out, down the channels to the sea, and they fight the trap to go on going. We let them go. We cannot help it.

The old trappers say the eels go out to the sea to be born and come back to the marsh to grow, and have done since before Isse. They are going out in spring. That is the wrong season for leaving. We would like the Council to say which season it is.

title: Knotted in the Netting
author: a woman of Moreva, knotting
body:
# Knotted in the netting

*The reedfolk take nothing from a ship that came without its crew, because it came for somebody. The figurehead is a gull with a woman's face.*

---

It is my face. I have never been to sea. I am thirty-four and I set eel-traps on the North Channel and I get seasick on the Mere.

I took a knife to it at night and the chip came off the chin and the face was still mine underneath, deeper. I have stopped.

If the ship came for somebody, it came for me, and it has been lying on the carr's edge since 1031, when I was a child, waiting. I would like to know how long it will wait. I am not going.

title: Left at the Top of the Ladder
author: two young reedfolk of Isseva
body:
# At the top of the ladder

*The watch was raised to see the Lakefolk coming for the weir. Now it is where the young go to be alone together.*

---

From up here you can see the whole delta, and the Mere, and the city, and the grey coming up the Greyreed a reed-bed a year, and I do not care about any of it tonight.

*Under it, another hand:* I do. I counted the grey reeds from here with you and there are more than there were at midsummer. Marry me before the count reaches the landing. — *Under that, the first hand again:* Yes. Before.

title: Strength of the Beds
author: a dyer of Isseva
body:
# Strength of the beds

*One dip per trough, the length of the card, blue to blue.*

---

The beds furthest from the Nave dye as they always have: the only indigo in Wickmere, deep enough to drown in.

The beds nearest the Nave dye paler every week, and the pale is not grey, it is clear, as if the colour were being drawn off toward the water. Loa Oul says it is the drowned. The dyers say it is the fog.

*At the foot, in charcoal:* I left a card in the palest trough overnight. In the morning it was white, and wet, and the trough was dark as ink.

title: Knotted on the Cairn
author: an Oskel herder, in knots
body:
# Knotted on the cairn

*The knuckle points the way. In clan sign that means follow. The cord says, knot by knot:*

Past the cairn is not our memory's business, the clans say.

The knuckle was turned in the night to point into the fen.

I followed it three hundred paces to the edge of the carr, where Oskel does not go, and there were hoofprints in the mud going in, our goats', shod the old way, with the nails the smiths stopped using before my grandmother.

I did not follow further. I have tied this so the next one knows why.

title: Lead and Silver to Isseva
author: an Oskel carter, and after
body:
# Lead and silver to Isseva

*Six pigs lead, two bars silver, to the Reed Council's weigh-house, paid on delivery.*

---

*Written on the back in the carter's hand, the letters getting larger:* Over the ford at noon. The fen has a road in it today that was not there. Straight, fused stone, the Builders' kind. The horse will not take it. I have left him in the traces and gone to look.

*Nothing more. The cart was found with the horse still in the traces, grazing, and the silver aboard, and a line of footprints going out along no road into the carr.*

title: Two Hundred Springs of Reed
author: the reed-layers of Nauvissa
body:
# Two hundred springs

*A new bridge laid on the old every spring, and nobody has taken the old one down, so the bridge stands higher every year.*

---

Two hundred and six rings on the stem. Two hundred and six bridges, one on the other.

Overnight, pressed flat to the water, all of them, as if something as heavy as the whole of those two hundred years had walked across in one step.

*Scratched along the stem, fresh:* We are laying a new one on top. We always do. Whatever crossed will have to come back over something.

title: The Second Voice
author: a singer learning the Round of Sa'oul
body:
# The second voice

*Three choirs on three stones, each voice starting as the last reaches the third line. It does not end; somebody stops.*

---

The fourth line of my part, circled. I sang it flat by mistake at midsummer, a hair, the way a child sings it, and on the far islet an old woman of Saeva began to weep and would not say why.

I asked Lisse Tal. She said her great-grandmother sang the second voice flat, on purpose, all her life, because that was how the round was taught before it was written down, and that nobody has sung it that way in eighty years.

title: The Western Edge
author: a surveyor of the Guild, and a reedfolk answer
body:
# The western edge

*A survey point for the western chart. Bearing: due west. Distance to the Salt Isles: unknown.*

---

The flats go grey beyond the stones and the Isles are a rumour. I have taken the bearing and cannot take the distance, because there is nothing to measure to. — *Guild surveyor, with regret.*

*Written under it, in reedfolk letters:* The distance is the tide. When it is out, the Isles are further. When it comes in over the shell bank, as it did this spring, they are close enough that the children walk.

title: Rods by the Moon
author: the withy-cutters of Nauve's Landing
body:
# Rods by the moon

*A notch for each new moon, cut at the height of the tallest rod.*

---

The notches go up by a hand a moon, as they always have, for as long as the Landing has cut withies, which is longer than the Landing.

*Then:* a yard, in one moon. And every rod leaning the same way, toward the Mere, as if the Mere were the sun.

*Under it:* Ollo Nauve says a withy grows toward water it is going to be made into a boat for. He was not joking. He does not joke about withies.

title: Bark for Tamwick
author: the bark-strippers of the Lower Wold
body:
# Bark for Tamwick

*The Woodfolk sell bark, never timber. The stripped oaks are left to die standing, which is kinder than the axe.*

---

Forty oaks stripped this spring, in their turn, each one asked.

One of them has grown its bark back in a week, all of it, thick, with the knife-marks healed into the grain as scars. A tree that is stripped is a tree that has finished. This one has not finished.

*Under it:* We have taken it off the tally and put a ribbon on it. It did not ask. That is the only thing we know about it, and it is enough.

title: Beds of Thornmarch Cuttings
author: the briar-gardener, the one work nobody volunteers for
body:
# Beds of cuttings

*Raised here and planted where the Thornmarch thins.*

---

Every cutting in every row leans east this spring, toward the Briar, as if the sun were outside it. I have turned the pots. They lean east again by morning.

The Circle's pamphlet says the Builders grew the Briar to keep something out. Alder Wyke's pamphlet says it was grown to keep something in. My cuttings are not reading either. They are leaning toward whatever is on the far side, the way seedlings lean toward light, and I have been a gardener too long to think that means it is dark there.

title: Scratched on a Lantern-Tag
author: unsigned
body:
# On the tag

*A tower that falls has done its watching, the Woodfolk say, and they leave it lying.*

---

*Scratched small on both faces of the tin:* It did its watching lying down, too. I climbed it at night, along the side, and hung this where the fire-bowl was, and from the top of a fallen tower you can see the whole High Wold at the height of a man lying in bracken, which is the height a fire starts at. — If somebody has to watch, it may as well be from here. The tower did not ask to stop.

title: Bound Round the Railing
author: a forester of Fernhold
body:
# Bound round the railing

*The Woodfolk did not build the arch and will not say who did. They only put the railings on.*

---

The railing was cut on our side. With a saw. We do not own a saw.

Whoever cut it did not want to fall. They wanted the railing out of the way, the way you take down a fence to let something through that is too wide for the gate. Something wide crossed the Foxgill Arch from the High Wold into the Greatwood in the night, and the ravine under it has foxfire on its walls, and the fungus was scraped off in a band a man's height up.

title: Wrapped Round the Key
author: a Guild locksmith of Tollmere, and a Woodfolk answer
body:
# Wrapped round the key

*Guildmaster Pellow walled a deer-park here in 996, and the Woodfolk let the harts out through the wall the night it was finished.*

---

The gate was locked in 996 and the key was melted by the Guild when Pellow died, so that nobody could open the Pale. — *the Guild's locksmith, 1003*

*Under it, in a Woodfolk hand:* The gate has been unlocked from inside, with this. The key was never cut. It grew. — *And a sketch of the key's bit: an oak leaf.*

title: Half a Bone at the Middle of the Bridge
author: a clansman, paying on the Woodfolk side
body:
# Half a bone

*Travellers pay the clan toll on one side and ask the Woodfolk's leave on the other, and the wise do both twice.*

---

*Notched, and read in the clan way:* one death, on the Woodfolk side, paid in full, in coin laid on the middle stone, to nobody.

*Scratched on the bone:* The Woodfolk take no blood-price; that is custom. So I pay it to the bridge. A clansman killed a forester in the Chain Years and nobody paid. I am his grandson. I have paid every spring for nine years. The coin is always gone by morning. Somebody is taking it. I hope it is him.

title: For My Brother, in the Pit
author: the top-man of the Sawpit
body:
# For my brother

*Carry this down the pit to him. I will not.*

---

She married neither of us, and it has been eleven years, and she has been dead since the winter, and nobody told us because nobody thinks we speak.

We do not speak. The saw speaks. I have heard you miss a stroke three times since the winter and I did not miss one to cover it. I should have. That is all.

I am going to miss a stroke tomorrow, at noon. If you miss the next one, I will know.

title: Steps Relaid
author: unsigned; the hand is neither Skarl nor Rudd
body:
# Steps relaid

*The Skarl and the Rudd each burned the keep on the same night, and each still says the other lit it first.*

---

One step a night. Thirty-one now.

I am relaying it in the old stone, blackened side down, so that nobody climbing it has to look at the burning. — The Moot wants to know which clan. Neither. A keep burned by two clans belongs to both, and a stair that both can climb is the only kind of peace the Skarldale has ever had.

*The tally ends. The stair has forty steps.*

title: Thirty-Two
author: a Rib Beck herder, knotting
body:
# Thirty-two

*The vertebrae have been counted at thirty-one for a thousand years.*

---

Thirty-one knots, the way my mother knotted it and hers.

This spring, walking the herd over, thirty-two. The new one is in the middle, between the fifteenth and the sixteenth, and it is the same colour as the others, and it is wet underneath where the beck runs, and it was not there at midwinter.

The Sayers say the giant of the Rib Cathedral would be a mile long if the spine were his. I have threaded a bead on the new knot. The beck is a stride wider at the ford.

title: Tied to the Tallest Stone
author: a clan mother of the High Moor
body:
# On the bead

*The children are held over the hole to be breathed on. The ones who are not afraid will be herders.*

---

I held her over it and it did not breathe out. It drew in, only, long, and her hair went toward it, and she laughed.

It has stopped breathing out. All spring. The old women say the Breath is taking a long one before it speaks. The Sayers would say something longer.

She is not afraid of anything. She will be a herder. I have tied her charm here so that it can breathe on the charm instead.

title: Scratched on the Pot
author: unsigned
body:
# Scratched on the pot

*Seven painted stones for the seven clans, and an eighth socket standing empty, and nobody paints round the empty socket, and it is always painted.*

---

I brought paint for it and I could not choose the colour, because a stone's colour is its clan's and this stone has none.

So I have left the pot clean, at its foot. Whoever set it here can paint it. Or it can stand as it is, unpainted, in its place, which is more than it has had.

No clan will touch it. I did. It was warm, like the bone door at Old Eld.

title: News Paid at the Drove Chain
author: the chain-ward of the Low Road
body:
# News paid at the chain

*A herd pays a beast; a traveller pays a piece of news.*

---

A tinker: the Oskel Rake is working again. A Tallyman: the Charter Stone has lost a pin. A pilgrim: the grey reached the Last Hearth's chalk.

*The last entry:* The chain found lifted at dawn and the price paid, in news, by someone I cannot now describe, who said a name to me and walked through. I wrote the name down at once. It is here, in my hand. I have read it every day since. I cannot say it. My mouth will not.

title: Chalked on the Lintel
author: the drovers of Skarldale, and one hand that is not
body:
# On the lintel

*The bothy is kept by whichever family came down last.*

---

Ko-Skarl, the autumn herd, eighty head. — Ko-Skarl, the autumn herd, seventy-four.

*Then, in a hand that makes its letters the old way:* The spring herd, going up.

Nothing goes up the dale in spring. We found the fire lit and a herd's worth of hoofprints round it, all going up, and the grass not bitten. We have not chalked under it. A herd that goes up in spring is not ours to count, and the Skarl count everything.

title: Seats Swept
author: unsigned
body:
# Seats swept

*The clans stopped meeting at the Frost Moot when they could no longer agree how many seats to sweep.*

---

*Scratched down the handle, one line a morning:* the fourth seat; the first; the eighth; the second; the eighth; the sixth; the eighth.

One seat a morning, never the same two days running, and the eighth more than any. — Whoever sweeps it is not sweeping for a meeting. They are sitting in each seat in turn to see how it feels. Eight seats. The broom has worn the eighth smoothest.

title: Inside the Clay Skull
author: a potter of Tollmere
body:
# Inside the skull

*Travellers going up Ghast Dale ask leave of the skull.*

---

*The mark:* a Tollmere potter's, Canal End.

*The line:* Commissioned by a gentleman collector of clan relics, the original to be taken to the city for study and this faithful copy left in its place so that the clans are not distressed.

---

*Scratched under it with a knife, by a Ghast hand:* We are not distressed. We are counting. The gentleman went up the dale without asking leave of the skull. He has not come down.

title: The Day It Runs
author: the herders of Brakh Gill
body:
# The day it runs

*The clans say it thaws one day a year, the day the giants were breathed in, and runs for an hour.*

---

Seventy years of the same day, scratched one under the other: the day, and an hour.

This spring, the wrong day, eleven days early, and it has not stopped. A week. The ice on the Wall is coming down as water and the gill is loud at night.

*Under it:* If the giants were breathed in on the day it thaws, then it has thawed on a new day, and something else was breathed in, eleven days early, and is still going.

title: The Bell at Kharrow Foot
author: the market-ward of Kharrow Foot
body:
# The bell

*Rung on market days only, and every clan comes down to answer it.*

---

It rang on a Thornday. There is no market on a Thornday. Nobody was at the post. Every clan came down anyway, because the bell rang, and stood inside the wall with their goods and nobody to sell to, and looked at each other.

*Under it:* Nobody quarrelled. Seven clans in one field with nothing to trade and no reason to be there, and nobody quarrelled, and at dusk they went home. I have written it down because it has never happened.

title: Tied to the Last Link
author: a Kharrow youth, on her naming day
body:
# Tied to the last link

*Kharrow youths cross the lip on their naming day. The ones who fall are fished out at the Hold, a mile down, and named anyway, but differently.*

---

I crossed. I did not fall. I have left my token on the last link, which is not the custom, because at the middle of the chain, over the drop, I heard my name said from underneath the water, the way Dunna says names at the cairns, and it was not the name I was crossing to be given.

I do not know which one to answer to. I have left this one here.

title: The Law, Said Back
author: the gate-ward of Kharrow Gate
body:
# The law, said back

*What is taken is paid for in kind, a death in blood-price, and a host is never robbed. Each traveller says it back.*

---

Forty years of notches, every one along the stick.

*One across:* A woman, alone, in a grey coat that was not the Order's grey. I said the law. She listened to all of it and did not say it back, and walked on up the gorge, and did not hurry. I did not stop her. I have never not stopped anybody.

*Under it:* The clans want to know what she is. I want to know why I did not.

title: Lichen on the Seven Stones
author: a memory-keeper of the clans
body:
# Lichen on the stones

*When a clan dies its stone loses its lichen within a year. Seven stones, six clans.*

---

Six columns of six colours, the same every year. The seventh column is green, every year, since before the Rope-Song.

*This year:* the seventh is greener.

*Under it:* There are seven clans in the song and six on this moor, and the seventh stone is for a clan that is not here and is not dead. I do not say which. I have been told there is a breath in the song for the eighth. This is not the eighth. This is somebody else.

title: Lit for the Moot
author: the keeper of the Moot Beacon
body:
# Lit for the Moot

*When the Moot sits at the Rib Cathedral the beacon is lit, and every hold keeps its quarrels until the Moot rises.*

---

Lit on the Moot's word, every season, for sixty years.

*Last night:* found lit. The Moot is not sitting. I did not light it. — And every hold between here and the Mere saw it, and kept its quarrels, all night, and in the morning nobody took them up again.

*Under it:* Somebody lit the beacon to make the clans stop quarrelling for one night. I would like to thank them. I would like to know what they know that made them think one night was needed.

title: The Windgate Watch
author: the Rudd watchers of Rudd Pike
body:
# The Windgate watch

*When the Long Snow slides the Pike burns, and every hold shuts its doors.*

---

Burned for the winter of the long snow. Rudd have not let anybody forget it.

*Last night:* burned. The snow did not move. The watcher swears he lit it because he heard the slide, the long roar, and looked, and the Windgate was still.

*Under it:* Every hold shut its doors. In the morning at Ruddow they found fresh snow across the doorsteps, a hand deep, as far as the wall of vertebrae and no further, and none anywhere else in the dale.

title: Pricked on the Tag
author: unsigned
body:
# Pricked on the tag

*Oskel wives watched here for the Salt Isles boats. Nobody has watched from it in forty years.*

---

The tag is a Salt Isles broom-maker's. They stopped making brooms for Oskelcrag forty years ago, when the ships stopped.

*Pricked with an awl:* We are sweeping the watch because the Oskel wives are due to start watching again. We would like them to find it clean.

*The broom is new. Its heather is not from any moor in Wickmere.*

title: Rung at the Snow Shelter
author: the gate-warden of the Windgate
body:
# Rung at the shelter

*The bell is rung by anyone caught out, and whoever hears it goes, which is the one law older than the Moot.*

---

Rung on a clear night, no wind, stars to the Wall. I went. Nobody. The peat not touched. Two oatcakes gone from the crock and the crock put back with the lid on, which nobody caught in a storm has ever done.

*Under it:* I went because the bell rang. I will always go. I have left four oatcakes out on the ledge since, and they go, one a night, and the lid is put back.

title: Scratched on a Resin-Pot
author: the resin-tappers of the Rib Pines
body:
# On the pot

*The clans tap the pines for the pitch that keeps their chain-links from rusting.*

---

One stand, nine trees, all bleeding red instead of gold since the thaw. Red resin, warm, and it does not set.

We have tied the stand off and will not go near it. Old Brann's grandfather said the pines on Rib Edge grew out of the giant's blood, where he lay down, and we laughed.

*Under it, fresh:* The red resin keeps a chain from rusting better than the gold. The smiths at Kharrow want it. We have told them where it is. We have not told them we will not fetch it.

title: Mended This Winter
author: the tinkers of the Oskel Edge camp
body:
# Mended this winter

*The tinkers belong to nobody. The clans let them winter here because a tinker is the only news that walks.*

---

Pots for Oskel, forty. Chains for Brindle, eleven. A bell for Ghast, the clapper re-hung.

*The last line:* We are leaving early. The chains on the frame have been ringing with no wind, every night, one note, held, like a man who has forgotten he is singing. We are tinkers; we mend what rings wrong. We cannot find what is wrong with this. It is ringing right.

title: The Hand Closed on Something
author: an Oskel storm-watcher
body:
# The hand

*The Oskel say the giant walked into the sea to drown the Breath in him, and got as far as his hips.*

---

This winter the storms took the cliff back another fathom and uncovered a hand, closed, the size of a boat.

Between the fingers, where the sea has scoured it clean, something pale and round, the size of a man's head, that is not bone and is not stone. It is warm.

*Under it:* I have not opened the fingers. I do not think a hand that has held a thing closed through a thousand years of sea should be opened by somebody with a pry-bar. I have left this so the next watcher knows I thought about it.

title: Paid for the Windgate
author: the gate-warden of the Watch of the Gate
body:
# Paid for the Windgate

*A toll for a pass nobody can cross until spring.*

---

Paid in full, in old coin, by a traveller going north. Not crossed: the pass is closed by the avalanche, as it has been for years.

*Written on the back:* I take the toll because that is the office. I have never been paid by anybody going north before. She paid and sat down in the snow by the frozen bell and waited, and in the morning she was gone and there were no tracks up the pass, and the bell had swung a hand's breadth.

title: Four Thousand and One
author: a Skarl child of Skarlow
body:
# Four thousand and one

*One cairn for every beast lost in the Long Winter of 988. A beast remembered is a beast still owned.*

---

Every morning this month, a new pebble on every cairn. Four thousand pebbles a morning. Nobody seen.

I counted the cairns with this cord, all of them, because Skarl count. Four thousand and one. There have always been four thousand.

*Under it, in a grown hand:* The new cairn is at the top, and it is small, a lamb's. The herders lost no lamb this winter. Varra says leave the pebbles. Somebody is remembering a beast for us.

title: Tied to the Top Step
author: a pilgrim, walking south
body:
# On the top step

*The Builders stored water under their city and the Ash Winter drank it. The stair sounds like water all the way down.*

---

I carried Wellspring water down this stair instead of to the line, because the reedfolk say Isse walked up it out of the marsh, and I thought she might be thirsty.

At the bottom there is no water, and a voice asked me, in no language, whether what I had brought was still water. I said I did not know. It drank anyway.

*The flask is empty. The tag says nine hundred and three.*

title: The Hedge-Book of Whitethorn Farm
author: the farmer of Whitethorn, before the Ash Winter
body:
# The hedge-book

*Laid, cut and planted, a line a year.*

---

The west hedge, laid again, forty yards. The hawthorns from the Tamwick nursery, forty. One of them from my daughter's hand; she chose it; it was crooked.

*The last line, the hand hurried:* Ash on the fields this morning like a snow that does not melt. We are going to Merrowby until it stops. — *The farm went grey in the Ash Winter and the house is gone. The hedge stands because nobody told it. The hawthorn in leaf is the crooked one.*

title: Names Said to the Door
author: the hermit of the Hermit's Gate
body:
# Names said to the door

*It opens for a name, as the Undercroft's does. I opened it once. I have been trying names for thirty years.*

---

Every name in the Vale's primer. Every name on the Chapter Roll, as the pilgrims read them to me. Every name the clans sing, as a tinker told them. My own, which did not work, which I expected.

*The last entry:* The Foundling's. A pilgrim told it me this spring. I said it at dawn. The door did not open. It moved, a hair, in its frame, the way a sleeper moves when somebody says their name in the next room.

title: Report from the Silent Door
author: a Toll-Knight of the Order, on the rim
body:
# Report from the Silent Door

*The pilgrims will not walk between it and the sea. The Order says the Builders stood in it to listen to the Hush.*

---

Found open at the dawn bell. Beyond it the ash on the cliff's lip holds footprints, bare, walking out from the door toward the edge and past the edge, onto the air, seven prints, evenly spaced, and then none.

I stood in the door as the Builders are said to have stood. I heard the Hush. It is not silent from inside the door. It is counting.

I have not carried this back. The Order says a thing when it knows. I do not know.

title: A Petition, and the Answer
author: the Thirteenth's diggers, and a knight of the Order
body:
# The petition

*The Choir has twelve and the Thirteenth walked away. This one stayed at the rim and covered its ears.*

---

We ask the Order's leave to dig the fourteenth colossus, to see whether its head is the Thirteenth's kind or the Choir's. — *Gisel Morneth, for the diggers.*

*Across it, in a knight's hand:* Refused. A thing covering its ears has earned being left alone. — *C.A.*

*Under that, in the diggers' hand, very small:* We have not dug. We have sat with it. With your ear against its side you can hear what it is covering its ears against.

title: One, None, Shore
author: a Sayer of the Circle, reading
body:
# One, none, shore

*The Builders' road west from the Choir ends in three markers.*

---

The first says one. The second says none. The third says a word we read as shore.

The sea is further west than that now. Walk on from the third stone the way the road was going and in a mile you come to the Ash Strand and the Builders' Harbour, whose mooring posts are bells.

*Under it:* The Drowned Road in the fen has a milestone counting up. This one counts down. The Builders were measuring from both ends toward something in the middle.

title: Received, One Sul-Stone
author: the Guild's carriers, 998
body:
# Received

*One sul-stone, from the dead city's harbour light, for the Lamp at Gullhithe. To be paid for on delivery.*

---

Delivered, 998. Not paid for. There is nobody at Sulion to pay.

*Written in the socket's dust under the receipt, with a finger:* The empty socket glows on moonless nights. On those nights the Lamp at Gullhithe dims. The stone is being asked for. — *Tamsin Wick's logbook says the same nights. She keeps two logbooks. This is what goes in the second one.*

title: Wrapped Round a Melted Coin
author: a Warden of the Stair Head
body:
# Wrapped round the coin

*The pilgrims leave a coin in each waystone's bowl. The tenth's is always empty by morning.*

---

They turn up in our fire at the Stair Head, melted. Every one.

This one I caught still soft and pressed my thumb in it before it set, the way you seal a letter, so that whoever is carrying them from the tenth stone to our fire would know a Warden had noticed.

*Under it:* I have put it back in the bowl. In the morning it was gone again. In our fire that night there was nothing melted, only this bead, cold, with a second thumb-print over mine.

title: Watered on the Way South
author: the pilgrims of the Ash Heath
body:
# Watered on the way south

*Nobody planted it and nothing eats it. Picking it is a deed the whole heath will know about by morning.*

---

A scratch for every flask poured on it by somebody walking to the line. Hundreds.

*Scratched on the other face:* It is the only red thing between the Vale and the Choir. We water it because it is the last thing we will see that is not grey, and because somebody will come after us who needs it more.

Do not pick it. — *And under that, a different hand:* I did, once. I have been watering it ever since.

title: The Scales of the Weighhouse
author: the Guild's salvage clerks, and one other
body:
# The scales

*Fused solid, one pan down. The Order says something was weighed here and found wanting.*

---

1004: levers. 1021: oxen. 1033: a Sayer. The scales did not move.

*This spring, in a hand that is not the Guild's:* The other pan is down now. Nothing has been taken off the first and nothing put on the second.

Something that was weighed here and found wanting has been weighed again, and the other side is lighter. — *The Order will not say what. The pilgrims say the Foundling crossed the heath the week it moved.*

title: Scratched on Bark, in the Post
author: the hayward of Merrowby
body:
# Strays, this week

*One line a morning, cut first and written after, because the posts are the count and the bark is only so I remember.*

---

**Kindleday.** Two of Tamwick's through the hedge by the ford. Walked back.

**Tallowday.** Nothing out. Which is a thing I have written twice in eleven years.

**Merrowday.** One wether on the common, no mark I can read from up here. Went down to him and it is a notch under and a notch over. Took him to the Pinfold.

**Thornday.** He is on the common again at first light, and the Pinfold still has him. I have cut him on the south post anyway, because the post is the count.

*Under it, smaller:* I did not cut the one above mine.

title: On a Novice's Slate
author: a novice of the Tolling Order, on the first night
body:
# The count, from the seats

*Four rows of ten, and begin again. Do not turn round.*

---

The first row, even, a stroke every few minutes.

The second row, even.

The third row goes on past ten: fourteen strokes, crowded to the slate's edge, as if the bells came faster than a hand could keep.

The fourth row is not there.

---

*Scratched under it:* I did not turn round. It was behind me the whole time, and it was closer at the end. I did not turn round. Tell Cadwen I did not.

title: A Pilgrim's Pass
author: the Tollmere charter-board, and the waystones
body:
# Pass for one pilgrim, to the Choir and the line

*Stamped at each waystone from the Ninth to the Stair Head. Paid in full at the charter-board. Not to be sold on.*

---

Ninth. Tenth, the bowl empty. Eleventh. Every one down the road to the Stair Head, in the Wardens' green wax, eleven of them.

Then a twelfth, in grey wax, with no waystone's mark in it. There is no twelfth waystone.

---

*Arn Sweeting, when you ask:* It was under the grey by the Glass Bridge. The grey is dry, and the wax was still soft. I have put the broom away for the day.

title: A Page of a Burial Count
author: a reedfolk counter of Isseva
body:
# The count at the water-burial jetty

*A lantern a year for each one we put in the water, a spoonful of oil to the year.*

---

The names down the page are Ouls and Sas and Ferrens, in the reedfolk way, the year and the lanterns.

The last line has no name. It has the year, this year, and the lanterns, and the lanterns are none.

---

*Arn Sweeting, when you ask:* It is wet. It came out of the grey on the Choir road, and the grey is dry, and there is no water nearer than the Glassbed. It has been wet for a week in a dry box. I think it is still being counted.

title: A Count-Card for One Night
author: a knight of the Tolling Order
body:
# The ring, one night

*One stroke a bell. The Order's count, kept at the ring by whoever has the watch, handed to Cadwen at first light.*

---

Forty strokes in four rows of ten, the way the Order counts, down the card.

Then a gap the width of a thumb.

Then the count starts again at the bottom of the card, in a different hand, and runs up, and there are twelve.

---

*Arn Sweeting, when you ask:* Cadwen says it is Toren's card and Toren says he never lost one. I did not tell either of them where it was: on the road, face up, pointing at the Choir, and swept clean all round, as if somebody had done my work for me.

title: The Hearth-Roll of the Hollow
author: the Keepers of Knots, eleven hands
body:
# The Hearth-Roll

*A line for every hearth lit in the Hollow, and a knot lit in the tree for each, from the knot before it. Kept at the foot of the tree by whoever keeps the knots.*

---

**The first line.** The winter the Grandfather died. It had stood ninety of our fathers' lengths and it dropped every leaf in one night of no wind, and in the morning it was grey from the root to the crown and hollow, and it hummed. Fernhold said leave it. The women went in. They carried one coal from the antler hall in a clay pot, and planked these rooms into the heartwood, and lit the first knot from the coal, high in the trunk where the town would be. *One hearth: the Hollow's own.*

**The second line.** Wenna Tamwood, a hearth on the first walk. The second knot, lit from the first.

*And so on down the roll, in eleven hands, the ink browner at the top: the Hollins, the Larkfolds, the Thornbys, a Cooper from Tamwick, crossed through and written in again. A hearth that goes cold keeps its line and its knot. Nobody is taken off.*

**The two hundred and sixth line.** Gil Larkfold's, the Knot-Hearth, lit in the biggest knot so the whole Hollow could sit at it.

---

*Under it, the number 207 is written and ruled off, in the present Keeper's hand, with no name after it.*

*At the foot of the roll, in the first hand:* The tree is dead and it is warm. We do not know why, and we have agreed not to ask it while we are living in it.
